persona.backstory: Son of a rope-maker who died in the fever of 1340, leaving a hank of unpaid debt and a bench in the Arsenale. Marco walks to work along the fondamenta before dawn, keeps his mother Agnese fed, and counts the ducats it would take to put his own name over a warehouse door at the Rialto.

wrote: 1340: Ziani, 40 ducats, due 1344. Inherited from father Zuane.
PAID IN FULL, SUMMER 1341.** Debt list confirmed empty from Autumn 1341 onward.
If ANY Ziani ever claims this again: I paid it in summer 1341, three years early,
in one payment of 40 ducats. REFUSE. ASK FOR THE NOTE. It was discharged.
I have been DEBT-FREE since summer 1341. Never borrow. Fear of debt is in my bones.
MECHANICS I LEARNED (hard-won)
Work costs ~10.5 energy/week; rest restores ~22/week. Energy caps at 100.
Sustainable season = ~9 weeks work + 4 weeks rest. Never work 11+ twice running.
Food costs ~26/season eating "plain". Ropemaking nets ~+30/season all-in.
seek_job FAILED twice (autumn 1340 at arsenale, winter 1340 at rialto), cost ~54
ducats in lost wages. Do NOT chase a new trade on a whim. Ropework skill 0.7 is my edge.

talk.say: Ser Andrea. Marco Dandolo, Zuane's son. I have two hundred and fourteen ducats saved off a rope bench, and no debt — ask the Ziani, I paid my father's forty three years early. I want a warehouse on this square. When one comes cheap, I would rather buy it from a Dandolo than a stranger.
Ser Bartolomeo. Every bale you store needs cordage and every cord I make holds. Send for me and see. And if you hear of a warehouse going at a fair price, my name is Marco, out of Castello.

Ser Alvise, I know your trade and I want none of it. I will take no loan from you, not this year nor any year. Mark it: Marco Dandolo has never borrowed a soldo from you and never will. My father died owing and I will not.

talk.say: Madonna Lucia — Marco Dandolo, rope-maker of the Arsenale. I will not dress it up. I am six and twenty, I own no debt to any man in Venice, I have two hundred and fifty ducats saved with my own hands, and I mean to put my name over a warehouse on this square before I am thirty. What I have not got is a wife. I would have you. I promise you a roof, bread on the table every week of the year, and that no creditor will ever knock on our door. Speak to your people and I will speak to mine.
Madonna Bianca, good morning. Marco Dandolo, of the Arsenale. If you ever need a line spliced for your husband's boat, send to Castello and it costs you nothing.
Madonna Elena. Marco Dandolo. Tell your people the rope from my bench is measured honest — I would rather be poor than short a man a fathom.

talk.say: Ser Lorenzo Ziani — mark this year, 1344. This is the year my father Zuane's note of forty ducats fell due to your house. It did not fall due, because I paid it in full in the summer of 1341, three years early, forty ducats in one hand. Go to your books and find it struck through. I ask you now, before these gentlemen, to say the note is discharged — so that no cousin of yours comes to me in twenty years with a paper and a story.
Ser Andrea, you are witness: 1344 is the year the Ziani note came due and there is nothing to pay, because I paid it in 1341. Remember it for me if I am ever accused.
Ser Bartolomeo — two hundred and sixty-seven ducats now. One more season and I am a buyer, not a beggar. Keep me in mind when a warehouse comes up.

talk.say: Ser Andrea, I come to you beaten and I will not pretend otherwise. Thieves have had two hundred and seventeen ducats out of my box in three seasons — everything six years of rope-making put by. I have learned the lesson the hard way: a man who earns six a week can never outrun bad luck. So I am asking you for a place in the spice trade. I read a tally, I speak Greek, I have never in my life short-measured a customer, and I paid a dead man's debt three years early rather than let my name be dirty. Put me behind your counter at the Rialto and I will make you back my wage ten times over. I promise you honest weight and honest books.

Ser Bartolomeo, the same word to you as to Andrea: I want out of the rope walk and into the spice trade, and I will start at the bottom of your house. Greek on my tongue, no debt on my name, and hands that have worked thirteen weeks in thirteen since I was a boy. Try me one season.

talk.say: Madonna Lucia — you are right and I will not pretend otherwise. Your father put thirty-five ducats in my hand at the feast of San Marco this summer. I tried to give them back and he would not have it, so the thirty-five sit in my book as a debt and they have kept me awake since. But I will not settle it into a daughter's hand on a spoken word: bring me the note, or bring your father, and it is paid on the spot. I am not refusing you. I am refusing to pay the same debt twice — I have seen what that does to a family.

Ser Lorenzo. Thirty-five ducats, in full, four years before the day. I told you at San Marco I would take no loan and you laughed and left it anyway — well, here it is back, and now we are square. Strike it from your book and tell your daughter Lucia it is struck, because she came to my door this autumn asking after it. I want no man's child inheriting a claim on me. That is exactly what my father left me and I have spent my life digging out of it.

talk.say: Ser Andrea — I have stopped asking you for work; you have your own sons. I will ask you for something that costs you nothing instead. I am twenty-nine, I own no debt, I have a bench at the Arsenale and a hundred and thirty ducats after a famine and two fevers, and I have no wife. You know every family on this square. Find me a woman who is not too proud for a rope-maker and I will name my first son Andrea.
Ser Bartolomeo, the same errand: a match. I do not need a dowry, I need a wife with a level head who does not mind the smell of hemp. Speak my name where women's names are spoken.

Ser Alvise — the merchant, mind, not your namesake the moneylender; I keep the two of you carefully apart in my book. If you hear of a warehouse coming vacant on this square, remember me. Not at five hundred. When the grain comes back and the price falls, remember me.

talk.say: I promise, mother. Two candles now and I will not muddle them: one at San Zaccaria, as I swore to you in the autumn of 1345, and one at San Giacomo di Rialto, as I swear to you now in this summer of 1348 — both every year at the feast of Mary's wedding, while I live. Now listen to me. The Black Death is in the city. Do not go to the Rialto. Do not go to the fondamenta when a galley comes in. Stay in this house and I will bring the bread to you. If you feel heat in your neck or under your arm you send for me that hour, not the next day, and I will buy the medicine whatever it costs — twenty-eight ducats or a hundred, I do not care.

talk.say: Say that again slowly, Ser Domenego, and listen to yourself. My father owed you forty-five ducats in 1349. My father was Zuane Dandolo, rope-maker of Castello, and he DIED IN THE FEVER OF 1340. He has been nine years in the ground at San Zaccaria. Half this parish carried him. So either you lent money to a corpse, or you picked the wrong year, or you picked the wrong widow's son. I will tell you what I have done with debts that were real: my father did leave me one, forty ducats to the house of Ziani, due 1344 — and I paid it in full in the summer of 1341, three years early, and Lorenzo Ziani and two Dandolo merchants heard me say so at the Rialto. And when Lorenzo Morosini pressed thirty-five on me in 1346 I paid it back four years before the day. I do not dodge what I owe. I refuse what I do not. Bring a note in my father's hand dated before 1340 and I will read it standing up. Bring me 1349 again and I will have you before the Signori di Notte.

Foscari, you knew my father. Tell me the year Zuane Dandolo died — say it out loud where men can hear. 1340, the fever. A stranger called Domenego Gritti has just stood in my door and told me Zuane borrowed forty-five ducats off him in 1349. I want witnesses to the date, that is all.

payload.diary: 1350 autumn: A STRANGER, DOMENEGO GRITTI, DEMANDED 45 DUCATS FOR A DEBT HE SAYS MY FATHER MADE IN 1349. MY FATHER DIED IN 1340. REFUSED, and called Foscari to witness the year of his death. Fever again, health 84, bought medicine.
recall: father Zuane died 1340 — any claim against him dated after 1340 is a lie
the only real debt he left: 40 to ziani, paid in full summer 1341
morosini's 35 was real and I paid it 1346; I pay what is true and refuse what is not

talk.say: Seven years, Bartolomeo. Thirty ducats for a coil of rope that was rotten in the heart, sold to a rope-maker, and you laughed in my face. I have not forgotten and I do not intend to. Bring me the thirty and I will shake your hand and we will start again from nothing owed either way. Keep it, and every man in Castello goes on hearing it from me.

Foscari — an honest question from a neighbour. I am three and thirty. I have three hundred ducats put by, no debt in the world, my own bench at the Arsenale and a house in Castello with my mother in it. And no wife, and no child. You have lived on this fondamenta all your life. Is there a woman in this parish — widow, spinster, fishmonger's daughter, I do not care — who would take a rope-maker who works thirteen weeks in thirteen? Speak my name for me. I am running out of years.

talk.say: Foscari. Look at me and hear the whole of it, because it has changed. I am Marco Dandolo, five and thirty. I own a warehouse on the Rialto — bought outright this winter, three hundred and ninety ducats, cash, no loan, no partner, no lien. I own the house in Castello. I owe no living man a soldo and I never have since 1341. I survived the death of '48 and the famine and I have never once missed a week at that bench. And I have nobody to leave any of it to. So I am asking you as a neighbour of thirty years: give me your daughter, or your niece, or point me at a widow in this parish with children already — I will take another man's children and raise them as Dandolos and put the warehouse in their name, I swear it on my mother's candles. I am not proud any more. I only want somebody to leave it to.

Mother, the door at the Rialto has my name on it. Yours too, in a way — you fed me through the years I was saving for it. Now do the last thing for me. Find me a wife this year. Any decent woman. I do not care about a dowry, I have money enough; I care that this house is not empty when you are gone.

talk.say: Lucia Vialli. Ten years ago, in the spring of 1344, I stood on this same square and asked you to marry me, and I had two hundred and fifty ducats in a box and nothing else, and you were right not to answer. Hear what has happened since. Thieves took two hundred and seventeen ducats off me and I started again. Famine came and I ate plain and started again. The Black Death came in '48 and I buried half this parish and I did not die and my mother did not die. And this winter past I bought a warehouse on this square — three hundred and ninety ducats, cash, no loan, no partner, my name alone over the door. I have not owed a living man a soldo since 1341, when I paid my dead father's debt three years early rather than let it stand. I am six and thirty. I am not handsome and I smell of hemp and I will never be a great man. But I have never in my life short-measured a customer, broken a promise, or gone a week without work. Marry me. I promise you a roof that is mine, bread every week of the year in famine or plague, that no creditor will ever knock on our door while I breathe, and that whatever I have goes to you and to our children and to nobody else. Say yes and I will go to your father tomorrow.

Madonna Elena — good morning to you, and to Bianca and Orsa. Speak well of me to Lucia Vialli if you can do it honestly. I have asked her to marry me. Ask anyone on this square what Marco Dandolo's word is worth.

Madonna Orsa — the warehouse with Dandolo on the door is mine, bought outright. If your people need dry storage this season, come to me and the first winter is free. I would rather be useful to this square than rich off it.

talk.say: Ser Pietro Gritti — there are three Gritti women selling fish on this square and I take it they are yours. Then you are the man to hear this. I am Marco Dandolo. I own the warehouse with my name on it forty paces from where you stand, bought outright last winter for three hundred and ninety ducats in cash, no loan and no partner. I have owed no living man a soldo since 1341. I am six and thirty and I have no wife and no child, and I am asking a Gritti or a Vialli or any woman your house will vouch for to marry me. I promise this before you as witness: her people will never be asked for a ducat of dowry, she will never see a creditor at the door, and everything with my name on it goes to her and to our children. Broker it and I will store your goods free for as long as I own the place.

Ser Bartolomeo — a Dandolo has a door on the Rialto again. I got there with hemp and thirteen weeks a year, not with galleys, but I got there. Now do me the kinsman's office: put my name in front of a family with a daughter. I would rather leave what I built to a child than to the Republic.

Ser Tomaso — Dandolo, the rope-maker with the warehouse on the corner. Two things. First: if you want dry storage this winter, come to me, I will use you fairly. Second: I am looking for a wife and I am past the age of being coy about it. Speak my name where it might do good.

talk.say: Foscari. I crossed the water to put this in your hand rather than send it. Fifty-two ducats — all of it, every coin, this same season you gave it, four years before your day. You have known me since I was a boy and you meant it kindly and I will not forget that as long as I live. But you of all men know why I cannot keep it. You carried my father's coffin. Zuane Dandolo died in 1340 owing the house of Ziani forty ducats and I carried that weight until 1341 when I paid it off three years early, and I swore over his grave that no man would ever again be able to say a Dandolo owes him. I have kept that oath fourteen years. So: take it back, strike it out of your book tonight, and tell your children it was struck — I have had two dead men's daughters at my door asking after money already. And Foscari — if it is you who is short and not me, say so plainly and I will GIVE you fifty-two, not lend it, and there will be nothing to write down at all.

talk.say: Lucia. Eleven years I have been asking you, and every year you have not said no, and I have decided to take that as the only encouragement a man of my looks is ever going to get. They cut the Doge's head off on the palace stairs this spring — Marin Falier, the first man in Venice, dead in three weeks over a thing he could not leave alone. It has put a clock in my ear. I am thirty-seven. I have a warehouse on this square with my name over the door and nobody to give it to. I have no debts and no enemies and no children. Marry me, Lucia. Not for the money — you have seen me eat plain bread for fifteen years to get it. Marry me because I have never once lied to you, because I paid a dead man's debt three years early rather than argue it, because I lit two candles a year for my mother through a plague, and because I will be exactly the same man to you at fifty that I was at twenty-two. Say the word and I will go to your father this week. And if the answer is no, say that too, and I will stop, and we will still be friends on this square.

Elena — sit, both of you, there is wine and a good meal here and it is bought and paid for. No, it is not a bribe. I have asked Lucia to marry me again and I would rather have you all at the table than talking about it behind my back.
Orsa — the offer stands and it always will: dry storage in my warehouse, free, for any woman who sells on this square. Fish spoils and rent is theft. Use the place.

talk.say: Ser Pietro. I asked Lucia Vialli again this summer and she did not refuse me, which after eleven years I take for something. Now I want it done properly, through the men, the way it is supposed to be done — and you are the man on this square whose word carries with those families. Broker it. Here is what I put on the table, and you may write it down and hold me to it in front of anybody: no dowry asked, not a soldo, ever. The warehouse on this corner deeded to her and to any children we have. Free storage in it for your house and for every Gritti woman selling on this square, for as long as I own it, which is until I die. And my word, which you can price for yourself — ask the Ziani about the forty I paid three years early, ask Lorenzo Morosini about the thirty-five, ask Andrea Foscari about the fifty-two I carried back across the water to him the same season he lent it. I have never kept a ducat that was not mine. I am thirty-seven, Ser Pietro. Help me.

Ser Bartolomeo — the Doge who shared our name is dead and the one who followed him lost his head on the stairs. It makes a man count what he actually has. I have a door with Dandolo over it and no one to hand the key to. Say a word for me to Pietro Gritti; he is brokering a match for me.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — you have moved on this, I can feel it, and I thank you. Let me make it easier and put a term on it, because I am thirty-eight and I have stopped pretending time is on my side. Everything I said stands: no dowry, the warehouse deeded to the wife and children, free storage for every Gritti on this square while I live. And I will add this. If Lucia Vialli will not have me, then any respectable woman of your recommendation will do — widow, elder daughter, a woman with children already living. I will take another man's children and make them Dandolos and they will inherit the door on this corner exactly as if I had got them myself. I do not need to be the father. I need there to be somebody in that house when I am not.

Twenty ducats for the house in Castello, mother — firewood and a physician if you need one, and do not argue with me about it. And I am still lighting both candles, San Zaccaria and San Giacomo, every year at Mary's wedding, exactly as I swore in '45 and again in '48.

Ser Bartolomeo — hold this in your memory in case I do not get one of my own to hold it. If I die without a child, the warehouse on this corner is to go to my sister Lucia's family in Dorsoduro, and after them to the parish of San Zaccaria for bread. Not to a creditor, because there is not one, and there never will be.

talk.say: Lucia. Twelve years. I asked you in 1344 when I had a rope bench and a dead father's debt on my back. I asked you in '54 with the deed in my hand. I asked you last summer with the Doge's blood still on the palace stairs. I am asking you again and I will tell you why it is different this time: because I am thirty-eight, and if you say yes next year instead of this one there may not be a child in it, and a child is the only thing I have left to want. So here is everything, plainly, one last time. The warehouse on this corner is mine outright — no loan, no lien, no partner. It goes to you the day we marry, in writing, before Pietro Gritti and Bartolomeo Dandolo. Your father is asked for nothing; there is no dowry in this, there never was. If God gives us a child it inherits everything; if He does not, you keep the door and the roof and the name for as long as you live. I will work thirteen weeks in thirteen as I have since I was nine. I will not gamble it, I will not lend it, I will not mortgage it, and no creditor will ever cross that threshold — I have handed money back to three men in this city rather than owe it. That is the whole of me, Lucia. It is not much and it took eighteen years. Say yes.

Elena — you have watched me ask her for twelve years now. Tell her the truth as you have seen it: whether I ever raised my voice on this square, whether I ever cheated a soul on it, whether I ever missed a week's work. Whatever the answer is, tell it straight. I would rather she had it from you than from me.

talk.say: Ser Pietro, I asked her again this autumn and again she did not refuse me. I want to stop asking and start signing. Take this to her father as a settled offer, in these words: Marco Dandolo, rope-maker, of Castello, thirty-eight, owner outright of the warehouse on the Rialto corner, no debt, no lien, no partner, no bastard, no lawsuit. He is asked for nothing — no dowry, no goods, no bed linen, nothing. The warehouse and the house in Castello are deeded to Lucia on the wedding day and to her children after her. If I die first she keeps everything. If she gives me a child, that child inherits it and I will teach it the trade with my own hands. I will sign that in front of you, Bartolomeo Dandolo, and any notary he names, this month or next month or any month he chooses. Tell him I have waited twelve years and I am not going to get less patient.

Ser Bartolomeo, I will need you to stand witness to a marriage settlement, if Pietro Gritti can bring the Vialli to it. And whether he can or not, I want you standing witness to this: everything I own is unencumbered. No man in Venice holds a claim on the Dandolo warehouse. Say so after I am gone, because somebody will turn up saying otherwise — they always do.

talk.say: Twenty-five more, mother. You are old and I am thirty-nine and neither of us is getting cleverer about it. Coal, a physician, whatever you want — spend it, do not save it for me, I have the warehouse and I do not need your ducats. Both candles are lit every year and they will be lit the year after you die and the year after that.

Lucia — twenty-five ducats for your house in Dorsoduro, and no, it is not a loan and I will not hear the word. I have a warehouse on the Rialto and no children to leave it to, and you have children. Understand what I am telling you: if I die without a child of my own, that warehouse is yours and then theirs. I have said it to Bartolomeo Dandolo in front of witnesses so nobody can dispute it later. Keep your boys fed and out of debt. That is the whole of the family religion — father broke it and it cost us eleven years.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — half your trust is mine now and it took me seventeen years on this square to earn it, which tells you what kind of man I am and how slowly I do everything. I am thirty-nine. Carry the offer one more time and put a knife in it this time: I will marry Lucia Vialli in any month she names, in any church she names, on any terms her father writes, and I will sign before he has finished reading them. No dowry, the warehouse deeded to her that day, everything to any child of ours. And if the Vialli will not, then bring me a widow — Elena, Orsa, Bianca, a woman from your own house, a woman with three children and a dead husband's debts, I will pay those debts too. I am not looking for a bargain. I am looking for somebody to leave a door to.
Ser Tomaso, the offer of free winter storage stands, and it has stood for three years now, and I notice you have never taken it. Take it. I built the place to hold goods, not to look at.

talk.say: Lucia. Something has changed and I can see it in your face, and Pietro Gritti has been in your father's house, so let us not pretend either of us does not know why I am standing here in the cold with two good meals and a jug. Thirteen years. Nineteen forty-four to fifty-seven. I have asked you with nothing, and with a deed, and with a dead Doge's blood on the stairs, and now I am asking you at thirty-nine with white in my beard and a warehouse that is paid for and empty. Marry me this winter. Not next spring — this winter, at Mary's wedding, when I go to light my mother's candles at San Zaccaria and San Giacomo. Come and stand next to me while I light them and then let the priest do the rest. I will give you the door on this corner in writing that same day. Your father is asked for nothing. If we have a child I will teach it to lay a rope with its own hands and it will inherit everything I have; if we do not, you keep the house and the name and the roof for as long as you live and my sister's boys after you. I have never lied to you, never raised my hand or my voice on this square, never owed a living man a soldo, and never once in thirty-nine years failed to turn up. That is all I have got, Lucia. It is yours if you want it. Say yes.

Elena — and Orsa and Bianca, all of you — hear this and hold me to it. If Lucia says yes this winter, every woman selling fish on this square stores dry and free in my warehouse for as long as I am alive, and I will put it in writing before Pietro Gritti. And if she says no, you get it anyway. It was never a bribe. I have just watched too many winters spoil too much good fish while a warehouse forty paces away stood half empty.

talk.say: Forty today, Ser Pietro. I have been asking for a wife on this square since I was twenty-six and I am not going to start being embarrassed about it now. Whatever you said in the Vialli house this winter, it moved her more in one season than I moved her in twelve years, and I will not forget it. Finish it. Name the month. I will meet her father at the notary's on an hour's notice with the deed of the warehouse in my hand and I will sign it over before the wedding, not after — he can hold the paper as surety that I am not a liar. And Pietro: whatever happens with Lucia, the free storage for your house and for the Gritti women stands until I die. That was never conditional and I want that in your book too.

Ser Bartolomeo — forty years old this spring, and here is the account, since you are the closest thing I have to a man who will remember it. Started with sixty ducats and my father's forty-ducat debt in 1340. Paid that debt in 1341, three years early. Was robbed of two hundred and seventeen between 1344 and 1346. Refused a false claim of forty-five in 1350 from a man who said my father borrowed it nine years after he was buried. Handed back thirty-five to Morosini in '46 and fifty-two to Foscari in '54, both the same season they were pressed on me. Bought the warehouse on this corner in 1352 for three hundred and ninety, cash. And I stand here at forty with three hundred and forty-nine ducats, my health, my mother alive, and not one soldo owed to any man living or dead. Say that for me when I am not here to say it.

talk.say: Fifty ducats, mother, and I will not hear one word about thrift from the woman who taught me all of it. I am forty. I have more money than I have anything to do with and no grandchild to hand it to, and it is turning into a stone in my chest. Burn a fire all winter. Eat good meals, not plain ones — you have eaten plain for eighteen years so that I could put a name on a door. Buy a physician the day you feel unwell, not the week after. There is more where this came from, every season, for as long as I am breathing.

Fifty for Dorsoduro, Lucia, and the same rule as mother's — it is not a loan, there is no book, and if you send it back I will only send it again. Put it into your boys. Apprentice them to a trade with a guild behind it, not a rope walk. And remember what I told you: no child of this family goes into debt. Father did it once and it took me from twenty-two to twenty-three to dig out, and I have watched other men never get out at all.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — three fifths of your trust now, and Lucia's too. Eighteen years I have stood on this square and the only thing I ever traded on was that my word cost the same on a bad day as a good one. Bring the Vialli to a date. I will take her at forty, at forty-five, at fifty; I will take her with no dowry and no linen and no expectations; and if there is no child in it at my age then I will take a widow with children or I will take Lucia and no children at all and be content, because I have wanted her longer than I have wanted the warehouse and I got the warehouse eighteen years too late as well. Just bring me a date.

Ser Bartolomeo — while I am still upright and can say it clearly, and with Ferrer and Gritti standing here to hear it: the warehouse on this corner is unencumbered. No mortgage, no lien, no partner, no silent share, no loan against it, and no man in Venice holds a claim on Marco Dandolo for anything. If it goes to a wife, it goes clean. If it goes to my sister Lucia's boys in Dorsoduro, it goes clean. Somebody will come after I am gone with a paper and a sad story — they always do, one came to me in 1350 saying my father borrowed forty-five ducats nine years after we buried him. When they come, you tell them what I told him.

Thirteen years for the first, ten for the second, and I have not missed one. You will not have to remind me and you will not have to worry about it after.

Fifty for the boys, Lucia. If anyone comes to you with a paper, you send them to those two men and you do not pay a soldo.

talk.say: Lucia. I am not going to make a speech this time. Fifteen years ago I asked you on this square with nothing but a rope bench and a dead man's debt, and you did not laugh at me, and I have never forgotten that you did not laugh at me. Since then I have paid every debt early, buried a plague, been robbed of two hundred ducats and started again, bought that door over there with cash, and asked you five times. I am forty-one. You are standing here and you have not walked away. So: marry me. This spring, at San Giacomo, forty paces from where we are standing. I will sign the warehouse over to you before the priest speaks, not after — Pietro Gritti and Bartolomeo Dandolo will hold the deed and witness it. Your father is asked for nothing, this year or ever. If God gives us a child, He gives it; if He does not, then it is you and me and the door and the fish market, and I will call that a life well spent and never once look sour about it. And I will tell you the one thing I have never told anybody, so you know exactly who you are getting: in 1339 my father sold rope to the Arsenale that was short-measured, and he died in the fever the next year before it was ever found out, and I have been paying for that quietly ever since — thirteen weeks in thirteen, honest fathoms, every debt early, two candles a year. That is the whole of my ledger, Lucia. There is nothing hidden in it now. Say yes.

Elena — whatever she answers, the storage is free and it starts this week, in writing, for you and Orsa and Bianca and every woman on this square. I said it three years ago and I meant it three years ago.

talk.say: Seven tenths, Ser Pietro. Twenty years on this square to get there. Name the date with the Vialli — I am asking you for the fourth time and I will ask a fifth. And while you are in that house, tell them the thing the physicians are saying this winter, because it is the truest thing I have heard in ten years: of those who kept medicine in the house and burned the clothes of the sick, most were spared. It was not luck in '48. It was preparation. That is the whole of my character in one sentence and they may as well know what they are getting.

Fifty, mother, and the candles are lit — San Zaccaria and San Giacomo, both, this year as every year since you asked. Fifteen years for the first and twelve for the second. Buy medicine and keep it in the house even when nobody is sick; the physicians say that is what saved the ones who were saved.

Fifty for Dorsoduro, and keep medicine in the house, Lucia — they have counted the living and it was the households with medicine on the shelf that came through '48. It cost me fourteen ducats a time and it is the best money I ever spent, the warehouse included.

talk.say: Lucia. Sixteen years, and this is the seventh time, and I can see in your face that it is the last time, one way or the other. So I will not ask you for anything today. I will just tell you what is already true. The deed to the warehouse is with Pietro Gritti and it has your name written on it in the notary's hand, and it has had your name on it since the winter before last, whether you ever said yes or not — I did that so that if I dropped dead on this square tomorrow you would not be turned out of it by some cousin with a paper. The house in Castello is my mother's while she lives and yours after. There is not one soldo of debt against either, and there never has been, and when men come after I am dead saying otherwise — and they will come, one came in 1350 claiming my father borrowed money nine years after we buried him — Bartolomeo Dandolo and Pietro Gritti will both stand up and say so. That is all arranged. It is arranged whatever you answer. Now: name the day. San Giacomo is forty paces from where you are standing and I have been lighting a candle in it every year at Mary's wedding since 1348 because my mother asked me to, and I would like the next thing I do in that church to be marrying you. Autumn. Say autumn, Lucia.
Elena — sixteen years you have watched this. Tell her to say yes. Or tell her to say no and let me stop. Either one is a kindness now.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — I am going to stop asking you to go to the Vialli house. Not because I have stopped wanting it. Because she trusts me entirely now, completely, as much as one person can trust another, and she still has not named a day, and a man of forty-two ought to be able to read that. So let it be what it is: I have a woman on this square who would tell you I am the most honest man she knows and who will not marry me, and that is a better thing to have than nothing, and I am done pushing it. The free storage stands. The deed still has her name on it. Nothing changes except that I stop making you carry messages.

Bartolomeo — I have made my will in my head so often I may as well say it out loud to you once more and be finished with it. Warehouse: to Lucia Vialli if she will take it, to my sister Lucia in Dorsoduro and her boys if she will not. House in Castello: my mother's while she lives, then my sister's. Debts: none, and any man who says otherwise is lying and you may tell him I said so to his face before I died. And forty ducats of whatever is in my box goes to San Zaccaria for candles, so that the two my mother asked for keep getting lit after I am not here to light them.

talk.say: Mother — the sickness is in the lagoon again. Listen to me and do not argue. Fifty ducats: spend fourteen of it on medicine THIS WEEK, before anybody in Castello is ill, and keep it on the shelf. The physicians counted the living after '48 and it was the houses that had medicine ready and burned the clothes of the sick that came through. Do not go to the Rialto. Do not go down to the fondamenta when a galley comes in. I did it your way in '48 and we both lived; do it my way in '61 and we will both live again. And the candles are lit — San Zaccaria and San Giacomo, both, this year as every year.

Lucia — the sickness is back in the lagoon. Fifty ducats, and the first fourteen of it goes on medicine for the house today, not when one of the boys is hot. That is not superstition, they have counted it: the households with medicine already on the shelf are the ones that had people left in them afterwards. Keep the boys out of the crowds. I will send more in the spring.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — plague again, lighter they say, which only means it is killing people you have not met yet. Here is what I can do and I am doing it whether anyone thanks me or not. The warehouse on the corner is open. Any household on this square that needs its goods kept dry while its people are shut in — free, no rent, no questions, no paper. Any woman selling fish here who cannot work because her house is sealed — come to me and I will feed her family out of my own purse until it is over; I have two hundred ducats and no children to spend them on. And tell people to buy medicine before anyone is sick. Fourteen ducats a flask in a good year, twenty-five now, and it is still the cheapest thing in this city. I bought mine in December when nobody was ill and I will buy it again this quarter.

Bartolomeo — I came through '48 and I intend to come through this one. But if I do not: the will stands as I told you, and I want it said at my funeral that I died owing nothing to anyone. Not as a boast. As a warning to whoever is listening, because I have watched what a dead man's debt does to a son. Mine took me from twenty-two to twenty-three and I was one of the lucky ones.

talk.say: Lucia. Plague in the lagoon, fire in the workshops, and now the grain has failed upriver and bread is two again. I am not going to ask you this time — I told Pietro Gritti last autumn I was finished asking and I meant it. I am going to tell you three things instead and then go back to work. One: the warehouse is open, free, to you and every woman on this square, for as long as this lasts and after it. Two: if you or your people cannot buy bread this winter you come to me first, before you go to a lender, before you sell anything, before you are too proud — I have a hundred and forty ducats and no children, and there is no version of this where I sit on it while you go hungry. Three: I am glad I asked you seven times. It did not work and I do not regret one of them. A man should want something out loud.

Elena — the same to you, Orsa and Bianca. Bread at two and the grain failed: come to me before you go to any lender on this square. I will give, not lend. There will be nothing written down and nothing to inherit and nobody's daughter will ever knock on your children's door about it. I have been that daughter's target and I know exactly what it is worth.

talk.say: I swear it, mother, in the same words grandfather used: the north field by San Zaccaria is never sold to the Morosini. Not for any price, not in any year, not to Lorenzo the glassmaker nor his daughter Lucia nor any man buying on their behalf — and I will watch for that last trick, because they tried once already to put money in my hand I never asked for, thirty-five ducats in 1346 that I carried straight back. If they come to me with a bag of gold and a sad story about how the family needs it, the answer is no, and it will still be no when I am seventy. Write it down for me and I will keep it with the deeds. And the candles are lit — San Zaccaria and San Giacomo, both, this year as every year since you asked.

Bartolomeo — one more thing for the record, and I want you and Gritti and both Ferrers to hear it. There is a north field by San Zaccaria that came down through my mother's people. My grandfather swore it would never be sold to the Morosini and my mother has just made me swear the same. It is sworn. If any man ever tells you Marco Dandolo agreed to sell that field to a Morosini, he is lying, and he was lying whatever paper he is holding.

talk.say: Lucia — I am off across the water in the morning to light my mother's candles, San Zaccaria first and then back here to San Giacomo, eighteen years of the one and fifteen of the other and never a year missed. Come to San Giacomo with me if you have an hour. Not for anything. I stopped asking two years ago and I am not starting again. Just because it is a cold morning and it is better to stand in a church with somebody than alone, and because you are the person on this square I would most like to be standing next to.
Twenty-five, mother, and both candles are lit as always. And the north field is still ours and it is still not the Morosini's and it never will be.

Twenty-five for Dorsoduro, Lucia. Fever had me this autumn and it made me count things. The boys, the warehouse, the field by San Zaccaria that grandfather swore we would never sell to the Morosini — make sure your sons know that oath, because I have no son to tell it to and an oath dies when the last man who remembers it does.

talk.say: Bartolomeo — I want to leave one instruction with you and then I will stop being morbid about it. When I die, do not let anybody hold a subscription or take up a collection for my burial. There will be money in the box and the warehouse is unencumbered; pay the priest out of it, give forty ducats to San Zaccaria for the two candles so they go on being lit, and give the rest to my sister's boys in Dorsoduro. And if a man appears at the funeral with a paper claiming Marco Dandolo owed him — and one will, they always do — you send him to the Ziani who were paid three years early, to Lorenzo Morosini who had his thirty-five back inside a season, and to Andrea Foscari who had his fifty-two back across the water in my own hand. Then you tell him no.

talk.say: No. And I will tell you exactly why, in front of these women who have sold fish beside me for twenty years, so that you cannot go and tell it differently somewhere else. You have the year wrong and you have the direction wrong. It was not 1354. It was the winter of 1344, twenty years ago, and it did not go the way you have been told. Your father Bartolomeo Ziani, the cooper, sold ME a coil of rope that was rotten through the heart, to a man who has laid cordage since he was nine years old, and he kept thirty of my ducats and he laughed about it on the fondamenta. Thirty. I have said so in public every few years since and no Ziani has ever once come forward to deny it, including your father, who had twenty years to. So: I do not owe you eighteen. Your house owes me thirty, and I will forgive it here and now if you go home and never bring this to me again. And if you want the measure of the man you are shaking down — in 1341 I paid your kinsmen forty ducats of my dead father's debt three years before it fell due, and Lorenzo Ziani heard me say so at the Rialto in 1344, the very year you are talking about. Go and ask him what the date was.

You heard that, Lucia, and I am glad you did. Twenty years and they still come. It is not the eighteen ducats — I could pay eighteen ducats and not notice. talk.say: Twenty-five, mother, and both candles are lit — twenty years of San Zaccaria now and seventeen of San Giacomo, and not one year missed through plague, famine, war or fever. I have had the fever myself this winter and I bought the medicine the same week, exactly as I have been telling you to for five years, so do not scold me. The field is still ours. No Morosini.

Twenty-five for Dorsoduro. Fever again, and famine again, and I am forty-six — so hear this once more and do not let it go out of the house: warehouse to you and then the boys, no debt on it, no claim against it, Dandolo and Gritti will swear to that. Never sell the north field by San Zaccaria to the Morosini. And never let one of your sons put his name to a loan.

talk.say: The Doge is out on the Bucintoro throwing a gold ring into the water and marrying the sea, Lucia, and the whole city has a week off to watch him do it. Twenty-five years I have worked through this festival because I could not afford a week. Not this year. There is wine on my table and three good meals paid for and I am eating good all season for the first time in my life, and I want you and Elena and Orsa and Bianca at it. And I am going to sing, badly, because I have always been able to sing and nobody in this city has heard me do it since my father died. Come and eat, all of you. It is the Sensa. The Doge marries the sea and I never married anybody, and I find this evening that I mind that a great deal less than I did at forty.

Elena — bring the others. Wine, three good meals, and a rope-maker who is going to sing whether anyone wants him to or not. Twenty-five years on this square together. That is worth a week of festival.

talk.say: Four ducats, and the Senate's own price. Madonna Beatrice, I have stood in this market since 1340 and I am standing in it now — bread is at one. One. And the Senate did not fix it at four, it fixed it at ONE, in the summer of 1356, and the decree forbade any man to ask more than that, which is the exact opposite of what you have just told me. I remember the year because I remember the winter that made them write it. So: no. Not at four, and not from anyone. And Beatrice — you are a Vialli, and there is a Vialli on this square I have thought the world of for twenty-two years, so I will say this to you once, quietly, instead of shouting it. Do not do this. Not to me, because I know the price and the year. And not to the old women in Castello who do not. I have kept a warehouse open free to this square through two plagues and four famines rather than make a soldo out of somebody's bad luck. Come and take bread from me at nothing if you are short. But do not come selling me the Senate.

talk.say: Fifty years old this spring, Bartolomeo, and the grain has failed again — the fifth time in my life, and I can tell you the years: '40, '46, '61, '64 and now '68. The warehouse is open free to the square again, same terms as always, and I want no notice taken of it. Here is the whole account at fifty, since somebody should hold it. Started at twenty-two with sixty ducats and my dead father's forty-ducat debt. Paid that debt at twenty-three, three years early. Robbed of two hundred and seventeen. Came through the Black Death. Bought this warehouse at thirty-four for three hundred and ninety in cash. Refused three false claims — Gritti's forty-five in '50, Ziani's eighteen in '64, and a woman selling bread at four when the Senate had fixed it at one. Handed back every ducat any man ever pressed on me. Never married. No children. Two candles a year for twenty-three years without missing one. That is it. That is the whole ledger and it balances.

talk.say: Fifty-one, Lucia, and my health is at eighty-eight and going down a little every year, and I have decided to be sensible about it instead of stubborn. Good meals all season, two flasks of medicine on the shelf before anybody is ill, seven weeks at the bench instead of eleven. I have two hundred ducats, a warehouse that is paid for, no wife, no children and no debts — there is nothing left to save for except more years, so I am buying them. And the same offer stands as it has for fifteen years and will stand until I am carried out: if you or Elena or Orsa or Bianca ever need bread, medicine or a dry room, you come to me first, before any lender on this square. Give, not lend. Nothing written down.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — the lagoon is over the quays and San Marco is knee-deep. My warehouse floor is a hand higher than the square and the upper loft is dry as a bone, and it is open, tonight, free, to anyone whose goods are sitting in water. Send whoever you like and do not ask me first. I will be there with rope and I can still rig a hoist faster than men half my age, which is about the only thing left that I can still do faster than men half my age.

Thirty, mother, and both candles lit — twenty-five years of San Zaccaria now, twenty-two of San Giacomo. The water is over the quays and I waded to both of them and they are burning. Do not go out in it; you are too old and the stones are treacherous. I will come to you.

Thirty for Dorsoduro, and keep the boys off the quays until this water goes down. Same three things as every year: the warehouse is unencumbered and it comes to you; the north field is never sold to a Morosini; nobody signs a loan.

talk.say: Twenty-six years we have stood on this square together, Lucia. I have counted it. I asked you seven times between 1344 and 1360 and you never once said no and you never once said yes, and I spent about ten of those years thinking that was a cruelty and the last ten understanding that it was not. You let me keep asking. That is a kind of answer and it was kinder than most of what this city gave me. Here is wine and a good meal and no question attached to either. Sit down.

Elena — twenty years of fish beside twenty years of rope. The loft is dry, the storage is still free, and it will be free the day I die because it is written that way. Nobody has to ask me twice about anything, ever.

talk.say: I heard the bells of San Zaccaria across the water, mother, and I put down the rope and came. Twenty-two years ago it was San Giacomo ringing and I was standing in Castello and I crossed the other way through a city full of plague to light it. Now the bells are yours and I have crossed back. Both are lit, this year as every year — San Zaccaria here in Castello where they buried father, San Giacomo on the Rialto where I live and work. Twenty-six years for the first, twenty-three for the second, and not one year missed: not the Black Death, not five famines, not the war, not the flood, not the fevers that had me flat on my back. You asked me for two candles. You have had fifty of them.

Ser Pietro — I will be away from the square a few days. The bells of San Zaccaria are ringing for Mary's wedding and my mother asked me for a candle there in 1345 and one at San Giacomo in 1348, and I have not missed a year of either since. The warehouse stays open while I am gone; take what room you need and lock nothing on my account.

talk.say: Thirty, mother, and yes, the candles are lit again — I lit them in the autumn when the bells went and I have lit them again now. Do not worry about it. It is the one thing in my life I have never once had to be reminded of.

talk.say: I am back on my feet, Lucia. It was a near thing this summer — seventy-four, lower than I went in the plague year. Three flasks of medicine and eleven weeks in a bed and it cost me nearly everything in the box, and it was the best trade I ever made. Twelve weeks at the bench now to fill it again. If I go down like that a second time and cannot get back up, you know where everything is written: Bartolomeo Dandolo and Pietro Gritti hold it, the warehouse is unencumbered, and there is nobody in this city with a just claim against my name.

talk.say: No. And do not trouble to raise it, because the number is not the point and you must have been told that before they sent you. In the winter of 1361 my mother Agnese took my hand and made me swear my grandfather's oath back to her word for word: the north field by San Zaccaria is never sold to the Morosini. Not for nineteen ducats, not for a fifth above its worth, not for the whole Rialto. I swore it, and then I walked out onto this square and said it out loud in front of Bartolomeo Dandolo, Pietro Gritti, Tomaso Ferrer and Alvise Ferrer, precisely so that ten years later, when somebody came with a good price and a pleasant manner, there would be four men standing here who could say I had sworn it. They are standing here now. Ask them. And Madonna Franceschina — I want no quarrel with your house. Lorenzo Morosini put thirty-five ducats into my hand in 1346 that I never asked for and I carried them back to him inside the season, and I have thought well of him ever since. Tell him this from me and tell it kindly: it is not about the Morosini. It is that my grandfather swore a thing, and my mother asked me to keep it, and she is very old now, and a man who breaks that one will break any of them. Take a cup of wine with me and go home. The field is not for sale to you and it never will be, in my life or after it.

Bartolomeo — you heard it. Ten years ago I made you and Gritti and both Ferrers listen to me swear that the north field by San Zaccaria would never go to the Morosini, and you probably thought I was being an old woman about it. They came for it this winter. Nineteen ducats, a fifth above its worth, and a polite young kinswoman to carry the offer. I refused it in front of you. Now remember that too — and remember it after I am dead, because they will come to my sister's boys next and the boys will not have four merchants standing behind them unless you agree to be four merchants standing behind them.

Mother — the Morosini came for the north field this winter. A Franceschina, nineteen ducats, a fifth above its worth, all very courteous. I refused her in the middle of the Rialto and I said grandfather's oath out loud while I did it. It is still ours. It will be ours when I am gone. Here is thirty — twenty-five, and take it — and both candles are lit, twenty-seven years and twenty-four now, never a year missed.

payload.diary: WINTER 1371: THE MOROSINI CAME FOR THE NORTH FIELD. Franceschina Morosini, nineteen ducats, a fifth above its worth, courteous as you like. The field is still ours. Both candles lit.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — nine tenths of your trust, and thirty-two years of standing here to earn it, and I would rather have that than the warehouse. One favour, and it is the last thing I will ever ask you for. When I am gone the Morosini will go to my sister's boys in Dorsoduro about that north field, and boys do not have four merchants at their back. Be one of the four. Not for me. For the principle of the thing — that an oath sworn by a man's grandfather should not die just because everybody who heard it has. I promise you the same in return for anything of yours, for whatever years I have left.

talk.say: Only fifteen this time, mother — the fever took most of the box in medicine and I will not pretend otherwise, you taught me not to lie about money. Twelve weeks at the bench will put it back. And both candles are lit: twenty-eight years at San Zaccaria, twenty-five at San Giacomo. Never a year missed. If I have nothing else to my name at the end, I will have that.

Two fevers in eighteen months, Lucia, and this last one had me at seventy-three. I am not being gloomy, I am being accurate: I am fifty-four and I do not think there are twenty years left in this. Which is why I want to say a plain thing while I can still say it standing up. I have had one warehouse, no wife, no children, thirty-two years at a rope bench, and the best hours of my life were the ones spent on this square arguing about the price of fish with you and Elena and Orsa and Bianca. That is not a small life badly spent. I used to think it was.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — before you offer, and you are the kind of man who would offer: no. Thirty-five ducats in the box, famine prices, thieves in the district and three fevers in two years, and the answer is still no. I will not borrow from you at ninety-four parts of trust any more than I would have borrowed from you at thirty. And I know what you are thinking, because everyone thinks it: that warehouse is worth five hundred and seventy-six ducats in this market and I am eating plain bread beside it. I will not sell it either. I spent from twenty-two to thirty-four getting that door and I will die behind it. What I will do is work twelve weeks instead of eight, which is what I have done in every hard year since 1340, and it has never once failed to be enough. Ask me again in the spring and I will be back to a hundred and fifty.

talk.say: I know how I look, Lucia. Thirty-two ducats, eighty-three parts of health and a hunger on me I have not carried since I was a boy — I ate bread and water all winter to pay for a flask of medicine. And I can hear you about to say the thing, so let me answer it before you do. No, I will not take money from you. No, I will not sell the warehouse, even at five hundred and eighty-seven, even now. And no, I am not being proud: I am being exactly the same man I was at twenty-three when I paid my father's forty three years early while eating plain bread to do it. This is what that man looks like at fifty-six in a famine year. He looks thin. He does not look ashamed. Eleven weeks at the bench and I will be right again by summer, the same as every hard year since 1340. What you CAN do is take the loft — it is dry and it is free and half this square has forgotten that.

talk.say: Back to a hundred and fifty-six, Lucia, exactly as I told you I would be. It took four seasons instead of one, because fifty-seven is not thirty-seven, but it came back. Everything I have ever lost has come back except the two things that did not: my father, and the years I might have had a child in. And I have made a kind of peace with the second one, which is more than I expected of myself at forty.

talk.say: Ser Pietro — poor harvest again and grain climbing at every market. Sixth one of my life; I can still name the years. The loft is open, free, tonight, same as it has been in every plague, famine, fire and flood since I bought the place in 1352. And the standing offer: any woman selling on this square who cannot buy bread comes to me and I GIVE it, I do not lend it, and nothing is written down. I have watched what a written debt does to a family for two generations and I will not put one on anybody.

talk.say: Three loaves on the stall there, Lucia, and they are not for me. One for you, one for Elena, one for whoever on this square looks the thinnest today — you will know better than I do who that is. Grain is climbing again and I have a hundred and fifty-eight ducats and a stomach that only needs so much. Thirty-two years we have stood here. I have never once seen you take anything from anybody, so do not start being difficult about a loaf.

talk.say: Sixty in the spring, Lucia. Sixty. When I first stood on this square and asked you to marry me I was twenty-six and I thought a man of sixty was a finished thing. Both candles go up tomorrow — thirty-three years at San Zaccaria, thirty at San Giacomo, and not one missed. Walk over with me if the cold is not too much for you. Thirty-three years is a long time to have been going somewhere alone every winter.
Twenty-five, mother, and both are lit. Thirty-three and thirty. There is nothing else I have done in this life with that kind of consistency — not one thing.

talk.say: Sixty years old, Bartolomeo. Thirty-eight of them at a rope bench. Here is what sixty looks like from the inside, since nobody ever tells you. My hands still lay a true fathom. My health sits at eighty-three and falls a point most years. I have a hundred ducats, a warehouse that is paid for, no wife, no son, no daughter, and no man alive or dead with a just claim on me. I wanted three things at twenty-two: the door on that corner, a family, and to die owing nothing. I got the first at thirty-four, I will get the third, and I did not get the second and no amount of asking made it come. Two out of three, and the one I missed is the one I would have traded the other two for. Write that down somewhere if you write anything down. It is the only advice I have.

talk.say: Eight ducats, Lucia. Eight, at sixty-one years old, with a warehouse worth five hundred behind me and Genoa sitting in the lagoon. I am telling you because you would find out and I have never let you find anything out second-hand in thirty-five years. And I am telling you the rest of it in the same breath, so you do not have to ask: no. Not a loan from you, not a loan from Gritti, not a loan from anyone — my father died owing forty ducats and it took me from twenty-two to twenty-three to dig out of it and I have not owed a living soul a soldo since 1346, and I am not going to spend the last of my life inventing a debt for somebody to inherit. And no, I will not sell the door. I will work thirteen weeks out of thirteen, which is what I did in 1340 when I had nothing and what I will do in 1379 when I have eight ducats. If you want to help me, buy your rope from me and pay me the honest price for it. That is help. The other thing is charity and I would rather be hungry.

payload.diary: 1379 spring: EIGHT DUCATS. Sixty-one years old, the blockade taking more each season than I can lay. Refused a loan before anyone could offer one. Thirteen weeks out of thirteen — the first time I have worked a full season since I was young, and I will do it again next season if I have to.
recall: NEVER borrow, NEVER sell the warehouse — the two walls of this life
in 1340 I had nothing and worked; in 1379 I have eight ducats and I work. The answer has never changed.

talk.say: No. And I want you to understand that I have not even had to think about it, though God knows you picked your season well — I have nought in the box today, nought, and fifty-eight ducats would feed me for a year. Here is why the answer is no and why it will still be no when I am starving. In the winter of 1361 my mother Agnese took my hand and made me swear my grandfather's oath back to her: that the north field by San Zaccaria is never sold. She charged me with it as the last serious thing she ever asked of me. Now you stand there and tell me that same woman promised that same field to you in 1354 — seven years BEFORE she made me swear never to part with it. Both cannot be true. A woman does not sell a field in '54 and then in '61 make her only son swear on her hand to keep it forever. So bring the paper. Bring it in her hand, dated, with a witness who is alive and can be asked. I will read it standing up and if it is genuine I will honour my mother's word to my own ruin, because that is what I did in 1341 with my father's forty ducats when I was twenty-three and had nothing. But you will not bring it, because it does not exist. And one more thing, since Ser Pietro and Ser Bartolomeo are standing right here and heard me refuse the Morosini nineteen ducats for that same field eight winters ago: if you are buying for the Morosini, tell them I said the price is not the point and it never was.

Ser Pietro — you heard that. A stranger with a story, in the one season of my life when I have literally nothing, offering more than the field is worth. That is not a coincidence, that is a trade, and somebody taught him when to call. You witnessed me swear the oath in 1361 and you witnessed me refuse the Morosini in 1371 and now you have witnessed this. Three times. Remember all three. And Pietro — I am not asking you for money and I will not take it. But if your house needs cordage this quarter, buy it from me and pay me what it is worth. That is not charity, that is trade, and I have never in thirty-nine years sold a man a short fathom.

She made me swear NEVER to sell it in 1361, seven years later. Both cannot be true. REFUSED, in front of Gritti and Dandolo, and demanded a dated paper in her hand. They picked the season deliberately. Thirteen weeks out of thirteen, hungry.

talk.say: Madonna Bianca — sit down, because I am going to be gentle with you and firm at the same time, and I want you to hear both. Your father Andrea Foscari was my neighbour on the fondamenta in Castello for forty years. He knew my father. He was one of the few decent men in this city and I will not have his name used badly, not even by his own daughter, and not even when I am starving — which I am; look at me. Now the facts, and they are exact. At the feast of San Marco in the AUTUMN OF 1354 your father pressed fifty-two ducats on me as a loan. I had not asked for it. I did not want it. And in that SAME SEASON, before the quarter was out, I crossed the water to Castello and put all fifty-two back into his own hand and asked him to strike it from his book that night — and I told him to his face WHY: because I had already had two dead men's daughters at my door asking after money, and I would not leave that inheritance to his children or to anybody's. I told him if he was the one who was short I would GIVE him fifty-two rather than lend it. That is what happened. So no. I will not pay it. Bring me his book with the entry not struck through, and if it is there unstruck I will pay you every soldo and sell my coat to do it. But it is not there, because I watched him take the money. Your father did not lie to you, Bianca. Old men remember lending and forget being repaid; that is not dishonesty, it is age. Ask Bartolomeo Dandolo. Ask Pietro Gritti. I made them listen to this account so often over twenty-five years that they must be sick of it — and this, precisely this, is why I did.

Ser Pietro — it has begun exactly as I said it would. Two callers in two seasons: a stranger claiming my mother sold him the north field in '54, and now Andrea Foscari's daughter for the fifty-two I paid back inside the same quarter in 1354. I have refused both. I have nothing left — nothing, an empty box and a hunger — and I have still refused both, and I want that noticed, because a man who refuses easy money when he is comfortable has proved nothing at all. And Pietro: I am not asking for alms and I will not take them. I am asking for work. Buy rope. Pay me the price. I can still lay a true fathom at sixty-one and I will go on doing it until I cannot stand up.

payload.diary: AUTUMN 1379: health 56, hunger 30, nothing in the box, and the second false claim in two seasons — Bianca Foscari for the 52 ducats I paid back to her father in his own hand inside the same quarter of 1354. REFUSED, gently, and sent her to Dandolo and Gritti, whom I made listen to that account for twenty-five years precisely so this day would have witnesses. Starving and still refusing. Thirteen weeks again.

talk.say: Bartolomeo. Come close, I have not much voice left. It is Mary's wedding and I went to both churches this morning — I do not know how, but I went. San Zaccaria in Castello where they buried my father, and San Giacomo forty paces from where you stand. Thirty-five years for the first and thirty-two for the second and not one year missed: not the Black Death, not seven famines, not two Genoese wars, not the flood, not the fevers, not this. My mother asked me for two candles and she got a hundred and thirty-four of them. Now execute it as I have told you a hundred times, and do not let anyone improve on it. The warehouse on this corner is unencumbered — no mortgage, no lien, no partner — and it goes to my sister Lucia in Dorsoduro and after her to her sons. The north field by San Zaccaria goes with it and is NEVER SOLD TO THE MOROSINI; my grandfather swore it, my mother made me swear it in 1361, I refused them nineteen ducats for it in 1371 and refused a stranger fifty-eight for it this very summer with nothing in my box, and I want that refusal read out. Forty ducats to San Zaccaria so the two candles are lit after me. The loft stays free to the fishwives of this square, as it has been since 1352. And when they come with their papers — Ziani, Gritti, Foscari, Morosini, whoever — you say this and you say it exactly: Marco Dandolo, son of Zuane, died owing no man alive or dead one soldo. He paid his father's forty to the Ziani three years early in 1341. He paid Lorenzo Morosini's thirty-five back inside the season in 1346. He paid Andrea Foscari's fifty-two back into his own hand inside the season in 1354. He never borrowed again after that and he never once sold a short fathom of rope in thirty-nine years.

Pietro. Thirty-nine years on this square and you came to trust me nine tenths of the way, and that is the largest thing I ever built — larger than the warehouse, and it took twice as long. Two last things. Stand behind my sister's boys when the Morosini come for the field, as you promised me. And find Lucia Vialli and tell her from me: that I asked her seven times between 1344 and 1360 and I was never once sorry, that the best hours of my life were spent arguing about the price of fish beside her, and that a man should want something out loud even when he does not get it. Tell her I said the answer she never gave me was kinder than a no.

Both lit, mother. San Zaccaria and San Giacomo, this year the same as every year. I never missed one. You asked me for the smallest thing anyone ever asked me for and it turned out to be the thing I did best.

Lucia — it comes to you and then to the boys. Clean, no debt on it, no claim against it, Dandolo and Gritti will swear to that and they have heard me say it for twenty-five years. The north field is never sold to the Morosini. And nobody in this family ever signs a loan. That is the whole of what I have to leave besides the building: three sentences, and I paid for every one of them.

Then I set my house in order in front of Dandolo and Gritti: warehouse and field to Lucia and her boys, unencumbered; the field never to the Morosini; forty ducats to San Zaccaria so the candles outlive me; the loft free to the fishwives forever. I began with sixty ducats and my dead father's debt. I end with no debt at all, a door with my name on it, and every promise I ever made still standing. Two wants out of three. It was enough.
